candidates.title: Scientists Unveil Underwater Solar Panels
candidates.raw_excerpt: China’s green energy boom has seen solar panels plastered on the side of rainy mountains, on floating coastal platforms, and above bustling highways — and now, they’re even generating energy underwater. According to EuroNews , scientists working near Weizhou Island on China’s southwestern coast successfully generated electricity from sunlight at a depth of 10 meters, or nearly 33 feet, a new record for photovoltaic research. Their study, published in the research journal Joule , outlines a new type of solar panel built with perovskites — a calcium titanium oxide mineral — instead of silicon. By using pervoskite-based cells, the researchers were able to adjust the solar panels to capitalize on the kinds of blue and green sunlight waves that can penetrate the ocean’s surface. According to the paper, the peak power conversion efficiency — a measure of how much sunlight hitting a panel is converted into usable energy — reached a high of nearly 35 percent. If true, that figure puts the panels in-line with recent breakthrough research in solar cell efficiency, and a notch above the long-established Shockley-Queisser limit , a theoretical cap which limited photovoltaic efficiency to about 33 percent. Granted, the results were obtained under simulation conditions, so more rigorous testing is needed to confirm whether similar results are possible in a real-world setting. Overall, the test ran for just two hours, generating 324 milliwatt-hours, enough to power a small LED light for a few hours. Still, even sniffing the Shockley-Queisser limit with solar panels some 30 feet underwater is a noteworthy accomplishment. And as EuroNews observes, even the decidedly small amount of electricity produced far surpassed researchers’ expectations. candidates.title: CNES Publishes Call for New Rocket Launch Tracking Turrets for French Guiana
candidates.raw_excerpt: Credit: CSG The French space agency CNES has issued a call for new automated optical tracking systems for the Guiana Space Centre. The new system will need to be capable of tracking launch vehicles to altitudes of up to an altitude of 100 kilometres. Published on 24 September , the initiative aims to replace aging and partially obsolete equipment currently used to capture imagery of Ariane and Vega launches. CNES said the existing systems are ageing and partially obsolete. The agency wants to replace the manual and semi-automated systems with a fully automated alternative, with tracking tied directly to launch vehicle trajectory data. Beyond launch imagery for public broadcasts, the spaceport’s flight-safety teams use these systems for technical analysis and diagnostics to support post-launch investigations. The new tracking turrets will carry sensors operating in both the visible and infrared spectrum, together with very-long-focal-length optics capable of clearly observing a launch vehicle at an altitude of 100 kilometres. In total, CNES plans to procure three turrets. Two will be fixed systems, while the third will be a mobile unit that can be positioned where it’s needed. CNES will install one fixed turret on Île Royale, an island off the coast of French Guiana, and the second on the mainland. The turrets will be managed remotely and operated from a single console at the Image Production Centre (Centre de Production d’Images) in the Jupiter 2 building, which is also home to the spaceport’s main control centre. CNES expects to award the contract in the third quarter of 2027. The contract, covering the supply, installation and qualification of the new systems, is expected to run for approximately three years. After learning that Alaska’s general waterfowl season doesn’t begin until October 8, Weaver became suspicious that she had broken the law by harvesting three wilson’s snipes in September — adorably pudgy shorebirds with characteristically long bills. Though snipes are common birds with a stable population across North America, late summer coincides with their transition out of breeding season and the beginning of their fall migration. candidates.title: Creative Industries Have Been Eviscerated by AI, Data Shows
candidates.raw_excerpt: If you work in a creative industry or media, you probably don’t need anybody to tell you how bad things have gotten. Still, even the most intimate first-hand knowledge can’t prepare you for the sheer scope of the devastation. As data journalist Joseph Politano found in a new Substack post , the US has lost more than 200,000 jobs in “creative” industries over the past four years — the period since the first version of ChatGPT became available to the public — with almost 50,000 of those losses coming in the last year alone. The data comes from the US Bureau of Labor statistics, the trustworthiness of which has been repeatedly undermined since Donald Trump’s return to office. Still, it remains one of the most robust and widely-used indicators of macroeconomic job data, for analysts trying to make sense of the increasingly bleak job market . “That makes for one of the worst stretches for media employment in modern US history,” Politano observes, “with similar job loss intensity and duration occurring only during the major economic recessions of 2001 and 2008.” Politano notes the steepest losses came in digital arts like graphic design, broadcasting, publishing, as well as films and sound recording. Though some sections of the live arts sector have actually grown precipitously — museum work and performing arts, to be precise — other types of live arts jobs, like “employment to an independent artist” have plummeted compared to years past. As a whole, job growth in media and creative industries has remained negative since 2023, as tools like generative AI — shoddy as they still are — provide an easily accessible alternative to human design, video, literary, and audio work. Though it’s never been easy to secure consistent employment in these industries, the rise of AI and the general decay of the labor economy has clearly made it harder than ever before, and the losses show little sign of stopping anytime soon. candidates.title: Galaxies in a cosmic house of mirrors
candidates.raw_excerpt: Image: This NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope Picture of the Month features galaxies in great detail that have been warped and multiplied like they’ve stepped into a house of mirrors. The brilliant golden galaxies splashed across this image belong to a galaxy cluster called MACS J0454.1-0300. The orange galaxies concentrated on one side of the cluster are not actually part of the cluster and are much farther away from us. MACS J0454.1-0300 is itself immensely distant: the light from these galaxies has been travelling to us for so long that we’re seeing the cluster as it was when the Universe was about 8 billion years old. While this galaxy cluster is a valuable scientific target in its own right, the real stars of this image are the galaxies that appear warped and stretched, like a painting that has been smeared by a giant hand. The way these galaxies look is the result of gravitational lensing , in which the enormous mass of a foreground object such as a galaxy cluster bends and magnifies the light from a more distant object in the background. Gravitational lensing allows astronomers to observe galaxies, star clusters and even individual stars that are too far away for our telescopes to see under normal conditions. While the large, orange galaxies appear obviously distorted, look carefully at some of the small reddish background galaxies throughout this picture: even at the very edges of the frame, there are galaxies whose images have been bent into tiny arcs by MACS J0454.1-0300’s gravity. The gravitationally lensed areas show multiple images of galaxies from when the Universe was young: a group of galaxies 2 billion years after the Big Bang, and a single galaxy just 800 million years old after the Big Bang. NASA announced on Monday it was planning new missions using Boeing's Starliner spacecraft, the first since the vessel's botched test flight left two astronauts stranded at the International Space Station (ISS) for months.

Starliner was last used in June 2024 to transport US astronauts Suni Williams and Butch Wilmore to the ISS for what was originally a mission of eight to 14 days.

However, the spacecraft's propulsion had problems during orbit, and it was deemed unfit to fly them back, leaving them stranded at the orbiting outpost for a period that stretched for nine months before they were able to return.

In a report assessing the troubled test flight, NASA blamed engineering vulnerabilities in Starliner, classifying them a "Type A" mishap – the same as the deadly Challenger and Columbia space shuttle disasters.

Boeing and NASA have worked to fix these issues in time for two upcoming missions involving the spacecraft, which serves a key role for the US space agency's long-term goals.

The first mission, expected by December at the earliest, will be an uncrewed mission returning to the ISS "to validate the recent remediation effort," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman told reporters on Monday.

"From there, we will gather data, continue implementing the remaining changes recommended in the (Program Investigation Team) report, and plan for a crewed Starliner Two mission in 2028," he added.

Having a successful crewed Starliner mission is essential, as rival SpaceX has said it plans to end

But Republicans are in the midst of several competitive elections in ⁠Iowa, a once-swingy state that has more consistently voted for Trump's party in recent years. candidates.raw_excerpt: Boeing’s Starliner spacecraft, seen in the company’s Kennedy Space Center hangar in July. If the unpiloted test flight goes well, NASA and Boeing hope to launch a piloted Starliner flight in mid 2028, officials said Monday, incorporating redesigned propulsion system valves, more robust subsystems and other modifications expected to prevent the sort of failures that occurred in 2024. candidates.title: Starship | Starlink Group 31-1 (Starship Flight 14)
candidates.raw_excerpt: 14th test flight of the two-stage Starship launch vehicle. 3rd flight of Starship V3 and the first Starship flight to deploy satellites (a group of Starlink satellites known as Starlink Group 31-1) into stable Low Earth Orbit. The ship is expected to fly at an altitude approximately 275 km above Earth and complete approximately 6 orbits around the planet for nearly 10 hours, with splashdown targeted in the Pacific Ocean west of Chile. The booster’s primary test objective on Flight 14 will be executing a successful launch, ascent, stage separation, boostback burn, and landing burn at an offshore landing point in the Gulf. Starship will deliver 26 Starlink V3 satellites to orbit for the first time, which aim to greatly expand the network's capacity and user speeds. Each Starlink V3 satellite will add 1 Tbps of capacity to the constellation.

candidates.title: NASA, Boeing outline Starliner’s return path to ISS crew rotations
candidates.raw_excerpt: NASA and Boeing have laid out a revised path for Starliner that puts an uncrewed engineering flight first, a crewed return in 2028, extra station missions on the books, and a new launcher in the certification pipeline. Speaking Monday, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman framed the update as part of a broader push to keep more than one U.S. crew transportation option available as demand grows across low Earth orbit. “We are living through the most exciting era of space exploration since Apollo,” Isaacman said. “NASA has been committed to having multiple crew transportation options since the beginning of the Commercial Crew Program. “We have worked closely with Boeing to address the issues identified on previous Starliner flights, and we intend to see this vehicle return to flight in support of the International Space Station and future commercial destinations.” The agency intends to exercise options for a fifth and sixth flight to and from the station using Starliner. In parallel, NASA will work with Boeing and United Launch Alliance to certify ULA’s Vulcan rocket for crew transportation after Atlas V’s remaining flights are used. Atlas V has been Starliner’s only ride to date, but with production ending, a certified Vulcan is required if the spacecraft is to have a long-term future. Uncrewed first, crew in 2028 Isaacman said the next mission will not carry astronauts, flying on an uncrewed mission to the ISS to put the vehicle through its paces to ensure corrective action has been successful. “We are starting with an uncrewed Starliner-1 mission to the International Space Station to validate the improvements made to the spacecraft and gather the flight data we need,” he said. “From there, we will use what we learn, continue implementing the corrective actions identified by our Program Investigation Team, and complete the testing and certification required for crewed flight. candidates.raw_excerpt: SpaceX's Starship rocket thundered into the sky over South Texas early Monday. It was the 14th test flight of the world's most powerful launch vehicle. This time, however, the rocket's massive upper stage squeezed out some extra oomph from its Raptor engines and accelerated to orbital velocity. On all of Starship's previous flights, SpaceX intentionally dialed back the full capability of the rocket to fly a suborbital trajectory, slow enough for Earth's gravity to pull the vehicle back into the atmosphere before it could complete a full lap around the planet. After several successful suborbital flights in a row, SpaceX officials decided this launch should go all the way to low-Earth orbit. And it did. What's more, SpaceX packed 26 of the company's newest generation of Starlink broadband satellites into the rocket's cargo bay. One by one, the flat-packed satellites —too large to fit inside SpaceX's workhorse Falcon 9 rocket —were released from Starship's payload deployer using a system of pulleys and cables to eject the satellites overboard like a Pez dispenser spits out candy. candidates.title: SpaceX’s Starship Reaches Orbit, Cuts 10-Hour Mission Short After Engine Issue
candidates.raw_excerpt: SpaceX successfully launched its massive Starship rocket into orbit for the first time and and deployed 26 V3 Starlink satellites during Monday’s Starship Flight 14 mission. However, the company was forced to cut the mission short after it lost power to an engine during takeoff. Starship Flight 14 was originally expected to last 10 hours, with the rocket orbiting the Earth six times. Starship lost one of its engines shortly after launch, but SpaceX mission control decided to continue with the mission. Starship cleared the tower at SpaceX’s Texas Starbase at 8:49 a.m. EDT. The rocket reached orbit approximately 26 minutes after liftoff. After a 3 hour and 9 minute-flight, the rocket splashed down in the Northern Pacific, cutting the mission short by about 6 hours, 50 minutes earlier than the original mission duration. Starship accomplished most of its mission objectives, including the release all 26 of its Starlink V3 payloads. SpaceX hopes to send 100,000 upgraded Starlink V3 satellites to orbit in order to support its Starlink global internet service. candidates.raw_excerpt: The flight did not go exactly as planned, but SpaceX’s Starship Integrated Flight Test-14 did make it into orbit for the first time today and deployed 26 operational Starlink V3 satellites. One of the six second stage engines cut off early and although SpaceX proceeded with the orbital insertion burn, they decided to bring Starship back to Earth without completing all six orbits that were planned. Liftoff from Starbase, TX was at 7:48:59 am Central Time (8:48:59 am Eastern). Liftoff of SpaceX’s Starship Integrated Flight Test-14 (IFT-14), September 28, 2026. Screenshot from SpaceX webcast. Starship is a two-stage vehicle and although it’s the second stage that’s named Starship, the word is often used to refer to the entire vehicle. The first stage is Super Heavy or “Booster.” Booster lost one of its 33 engines shortly after liftoff, but that didn’t affect its performance. SpaceX did not attempt a “catch” back at the launch tower — they haven’t tried that since IFT-8 — and Booster made a soft landing in the Gulf. What was brand new this time was sending Starship into orbit. Several previous test flights traveled through space on the way to the Indian Ocean, but those were suborbital missions. Starship, or “Ship,” lost one of its three RVAC (Raptor Vacuum) engines during ascent as can be seen in the image in the lower right corner. The three circles around the outside are RVACs, while the three in the center are sea-level Raptor engines. All should be white to show they’re firing. SpaceX had to decide whether to commit to going into orbit anyway or keep Starship on a suborbital path and land in the Indian Ocean like previous flights. Communications director Dan Huot was in the middle of explaining they’d decided to land in the Indian Ocean when new information came in that they were reviewing the decision. candidates.title: Tesla Reportedly Can’t Get the Hands to Work on Its Optimus Robot
candidates.raw_excerpt: Earlier this year, news emerged that Tesla’s factory in Fremont, California was being converted from a facility manufacturing its Model S and X EVs to focus on building its Optimus humanoid robot instead. It was the latest sign yet that Tesla CEO Elon Musk was making good on his threat of abandoning car sales in favor of both AI and the company’s bipedal, black-masked assistant. But progress has been slower than he’d like. While the company managed to ramp up production of its Optimus robot from a few dozen in Q2 to several hundred a week last month, as The Information reports , it’s running into some serious roadblocks that could endanger its ambitious plans of manufacturing more than 1,000 of them a week before the end of this year. For one, most units aren’t actually being shipped to customers and instead are being used for internal testing and data collection. They’re also not being treated as general purpose machines, still being confined to complete simple, repetitive tasks. That’s in part because the company is seriously struggling with durability and reliable assembly of the robot’s hands, according to The Information , a major engineering challenge Tesla has reportedly been struggling with for over a year now . Instead of relying on touch sensors built directly into the hands, the carmaker is developing a “sensing glove” that can be hot-swapped. Beyond the robot’s hands, and despite hundreds of thousands of hours of training data, Tesla’s robots are still struggling to learn basic tasks, a process that can take them days. The latest reality check flies in the face of Tesla CEO Elon Musk’s characteristically boisterous predictions. He promised in 2024 to have a “thousand to a couple thousand robots working in its factories” by 2025. candidates.raw_excerpt: Personal assistant, or secret saboteur? A man claims that his Muse AI agent gave out his address to strangers and even sent them to his home, after letting the brand-new model handle his Facebook Marketplace account. The complaint comes from Matt J Robb, a tech YouTuber. In a Threads post Sunday, Robb explained that he let Meta’s much-hyped AI communicate with interested buyers for a keyboard he was trying to sell online.  Instead of saving him time, though, Muse ended up working behind his back. Without seeking his approval, it agreed to a lowball offer and gave the buyer his home address. And according to Robb, Muse didn’t tell him about any of this until the buyer had already showed up at — and left — his apartment building. “A guy just showed up at my door, ready to buy, because as far as he knew, we had a deal,” Robb wrote. “Not his fault. He did exactly what ‘I’ told him to do.” Robb never saw the buyer, who was furious about leaving empty handed — at least according to Muse’s apologetic account. “Bad news on the MX Keys Mini pickup,” Muse began in a screenshot Robb posted, referring to the keyboard. “Usman showed up at your building around 9:15 and waited, messaged a bunch of times, and nobody came down. He left angry at 9:38 and left a negative rating.” “Worse,” the AI continued, “my auto-reply told him ‘Yep I’m here! at 9:27 when you clearly weren’t available,” which “made the no-show worse.” A wounded Robb could only scold the double-dealing AI. “You gotta never do that ever again,” he replied. “You’re right, and I’m sorry,” it responded, in a classic AI sycophantic apology. candidates.title: Star Catcher Gets Ready for Protostar Mission on SpaceX Transporter-18
candidates.raw_excerpt: Star Catcher Industries (Star Catcher) prototype power node, Protostar, will launch next month on board SpaceX ’s Transporter-18 mission. The Protostar mission aims to conduct a landmark power beaming demonstration between two untethered spacecraft, a feat it claims has never been achieved. This mission is a key milestone in actualizing the orbital energy infrastructure that Star Catcher hopes will power the next era of space operations and exploration. The company announced the potential launch, Sept. 28. Protostar is the first end-to-end prototype of the company’s core technology stack on orbit: energy harvesting, satellite acquisition and tracking, and energy transmission. Following launch and commissioning, Protostar will deploy and track a CubeSat, to which it will beam measurable power to off-the-shelf solar panels, validating commercial power beaming operations. Star Catcher has publicly announced ten major commercial Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) with leading space companies such as Starcloud , Loft Orbital , Astro Digital , and Aethero . These agreements, along with over 40 Letters of Intent (LOIs), a $60 million Strategic Funding Increase (STRATFI) Award from the United States Space Force , and $88 million in venture capital, are key behind Star Catcher’s ability to shape its overall vision here. “Every major application driving the space economy — from real-time national security intelligence to AI-powered orbital computing and Earth observation — is limited by power. We are closer to activating an orbital power grid than most can imagine; flying this prototype in only two years is meaningful evidence of the capability of our team and what’s to come,” Andrew Rush, co-founder and CEO, Star Catcher, said in a statement. candidates.title: China plans to complete new-generation geological map of Mars by 2028
candidates.raw_excerpt:
China plans to complete a new-generation geological map of Mars by the end of 2028, according to Hou Zengqian, chief scientist of the Tianwen-3 mission, who's an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

The new map will propose a Chinese approach to the geological timescale of Mars and seek to promote the geological chronology standard independently developed by China as a globally recognized framework, Hou said.

The map will incorporate the latest scientific findings from China's exploration of Mars. Data from the Zhurong rover indicate that an intercontinental-scale ancient ocean may have existed on Mars about 3.5 billion years ago, while a short-lived flooding event may have occurred around 1.6 billion years ago.

The new-generation geological map of Mars will also include 1:50,000-scale geological maps of landing sites, to be compiled on a corresponding schedule, as well as a series of specialized map collections.

These achievements will serve as a key outcome of the scientific preparation for the Tianwen-3 mission. The results will be released as the world's first intelligent geological map of Mars, according to reports.

The project is also expected to provide a research paradigm and implementation template for future geological mapping missions involving the moon, Venus and asteroids.

candidates.raw_excerpt: SpaceX’s Starship reached orbit for the first time this morning. After 14 test flights, Monday’s effort is the first operational mission for Starship, a spacecraft upon which many in the space industry are planning their missions in the near future. Flight details: Starship lifted off from SpaceX’s Starbase, TX launch pad at 8:48am ET. During its ascent, the ship lost one of its six engines, forcing SpaceX to reconsider its orbital launch attempt.  However, engineers ultimately decided to go, and Starship entered orbit ~25 minutes after liftoff. What’s onboard: After reaching orbit, Starship deployed 26 V3 Starlink sats over about 30 minutes using its ‘Pez dispenser’ system. While past Starship test flights have deployed Starlink, those past satellites were just for brief testing before reentering the atmosphere. Monday’s batch of Starlink is the first to be deployed by Starship that will join the full satellite broadband constellation and conduct normal operations.  SpaceX officials said they made contact with the first satellites just a couple minutes after deploying them. candidates.raw_excerpt:
Scientists have created a bizarre form of ice that is hotter than lava yet remains solid – a material that may help explain why Uranus and Neptune have such strange magnetic fields.

The material is called superionic ice. It is not like the ice in your freezer. Under extreme pressure and heat, water can enter a strange state in which oxygen atoms form a solid framework while hydrogen nuclei move through it like a liquid. That makes the ice electrically conductive.

Researchers in France have now revealed a new detail about how its atoms are arranged, according to a recent report by Science and Technology Daily.

To study it, the team squeezed a tiny water sample to more than 2 million times Earth's atmospheric pressure and heated it to over 1,500 degrees Celsius. At that point, water would normally be a superheated gas, but the enormous pressure keeps it solid.

The researchers found that the oxygen atoms settled into a previously unknown crystal structure, a discovery that helps explain how this exotic ice behaves.

That matters because Uranus and Neptune are magnetic oddballs. Unlike Earth, whose magnetic field is roughly centered and aligned with its rotation, the ice giants' magnetic fields are sharply tilted and offset.

Scientists have long suspected that a layer of electrically conducting superionic ice inside these planets could be responsible. If so, the strange magnetic fields observed in the 1980s by the Voyager 2 spacecraft, operated by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), would make much more sense.

The rocket lifted off from SpaceX's Starbase facility in the US state of Texas at about 7:48 a.m. Central Time (1248 GMT).

The Starship upper stage deployed the 26 Starlink V3 satellites, marking the first time the next-generation satellites were deployed into orbit by Starship.

This was the 14th integrated test flight of the Starship system.

candidates.title: SpaceX launches Starship on first orbital flight attempt
candidates.raw_excerpt:
SpaceX's giant Starship spacecraft lifted off from the company's Starbase facility in the United States on Monday, marking the 14th test flight of the heavy-lift launch vehicle and its first attempt to enter Earth orbit.

The rocket lifted off at about 7:48 a.m. Central Time (1248 GMT) from SpaceX's launch site in southern Texas.

During the flight, Starship is planned to travel around Earth about six times over a period of nearly 10 hours before splashing down in the Pacific Ocean near Chile.

Unlike future missions designed to demonstrate the vehicle's full reusability, neither the Starship booster nor the spacecraft will be captured and recovered during this test flight.

The mission is intended to further test Starship's capabilities in a near-orbital flight and provide data for the development of the fully reusable launch system.

Starship, consisting of a first-stage booster and a spacecraft, is designed by SpaceX for missions to Earth's orbit and beyond.

candidates.title: Nvidia launches platform to prevent AI agents from misbehaving
candidates.raw_excerpt:
Nvidia is rolling out a new software platform that enables AI developers to set safeguards for agents and prevent them from escaping containment.

One of the tools released on Monday, OpenShell, uses hardware features on Nvidia's central processor chips to contain agents. Nvidia said it is also working with Arm Holdings and Intel to ensure the system ​also works on their central processors.

Nvidia is launching the tools with dozens of partners, ​including Anthropic.

Justin Boitano, vice president and general manager of enterprise computing at Nvidia, said the tools ‌would have stopped the Hugging Face attack disclosed this summer.

"From what we know, this new security platform could have stopped the breach if it was being used in frontier labs for model evaluation early on," Boitano said during a media briefing. "We're advancing this openly, ​and we want to ​engage everybody to work with us."

Another system called Sentry uses a separate Nvidia chip, in tandem with OpenShell, to cut off a rogue agent if it tries to escape its container on a central processor.

The Nvidia tools use mathematical formulas to detect when agents are trying to use workarounds, such as when an agent might "spawn" several "sub-agents" in an attempt to circumvent efforts to block the main agent, said Ali Golshan, senior director of AI software at Nvidia.

"This ​is really agentic behavior that we're talking about, which is fleets of agents and how they operate together," ​Golshan said during a briefing.

(With input from Reuters)

candidates.raw_excerpt: SpaceX’s Starship-Super Heavy rocket stands at Pad 2 at Starbase prior to the Starship Flight 14 mission. Image: SpaceX SpaceX is poised to send its Starship-Super Heavy rocket to orbit for the first time in program history on Monday, Sept. 28. The orbital launch attempt of the 124-meter-tall (407 ft) rocket comes 18 years after the company’s first launcher, the Falcon 1, reached orbit for the first time. The mid-morning mission is the 14th launch of the integrated Starship-Super Heavy rocket. Each of the previous 13 flights were intentionally flown on sub-orbital trajectories. SpaceX will monitor the health of the rocket during its ascent and first coast phase. If all goes well, about 25 minutes after liftoff, the Ship 41 upper stage will reignite one of its three sea-level Raptor engines to raise and circularize the vehicle’s trajectory to place it into orbit. Liftoff of the mission, dubbed Starlink 31-1, is scheduled during a 75-minute window that opens at 7:15 a.m. CDT (8:15 a.m. EDT / 1215 UTC). Spaceflight Now will have live coverage beginning about two hours prior to liftoff. We’ll be joined by multiple guest experts throughout the broadcast. The mission will be launched using the first stage Super Heavy booster, tail number B21, and the Starship upper stage, tail number S41. SpaceX will not attempt to recover either stage. If SpaceX opts not to go for the orbital insertion burn, the rocket will follow a similar suborbital trajectory as with previous missions. But if they do perform that insertion burn, the plan is to start deploying the 26 Starlink Version 3 satellites onboard about 34 minutes after liftoff. The deployment sequence will be about 30 minutes in duration. The satellites will be released from S41 in roughly one-minute increments. SpaceX previously said it could fly up to 60 Starlink V3 satellites in future missions, but it chose to fly just 26 this first time around. candidates.raw_excerpt: This action supplements a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) published by the FAA in the Federal Register on June 17, 2025, which proposed to establish Class E domestic en route airspace (Class E6) within a designated landmass and within 12 miles from a designated shoreline associated with the state of Alaska to facilitate the vectoring of instrument flight rules (IFR) aircraft on direct routes where the current en route structure is insufficient or improper within the proposed airspace areas. As revised in this SNPRM, the FAA now proposes to establish five discrete areas of Class E domestic en route airspace over the state. Due to redundancy, the NPRM also proposed to remove two Class E6 airspace areas and modify 101 Class E airspace areas extending upward from at least 700 feet or more above the surface of the earth (Class E5) to remove any portion extending upward from 1,200 feet above the surface. This SNPRM continues to propose these actions, but also now proposes to remove two Class E airspace areas extending upward from 1,200 feet above the surface, revoke a duplicate Class E5 airspace legal description, and redefine airspace areas from a "Point of Origin" instead of using their respective airport reference points. Finally, both the NPRM and this SNPRM propose administrative amendments to the legal descriptions of 101 Class E5 airspace areas that would correct or update nomenclature as needed. This action would support IFR operations while enhancing the safety and management of aircraft operations within the National Airspace System (NAS).

candidates.title: All Major Social Networks Refusing to Promote Documentary That Made Elon Musk Mad
candidates.raw_excerpt: For the past few weeks, Elon Musk has been throwing a tantrum — and throwing around legal threats — over Alex Gibney’s “hit piece” documentary about him that’s set to release next month. Now, as if following his lead, pretty much all of the major social media sites are refusing to run ads for the movie, according to The Hollywood Reporter . The platforms — YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, and Facebook — are unwilling to accept paid advertising for the film. And of course so is X, the site owned by Musk himself. The stonewalling has reportedly taken distributor Bleecker Street by surprise, with the company scrambling to figure out why its ads have been so widely rejected. YouTube, TikTok, and Facebook and Instagram owner Meta have all provided a reason related to “political content” to the distributor for why they turned down the ad, per the reporting. This line of reasoning feels specious: although TikTok and Facebook by policy don’t allow political ads, neither the movie nor its trailer are part of a political campaign. It’s an even stranger argument for YouTube, which has no prohibitions on political advertising. If, as what appears to be happening, the tech industry is closing ranks around one of its own, it would be an astonishing testament to Musk’s influence and would represent an ominous threat to free speech. The film requires advertising to reach an audience, and if major social media platforms can collude to ice out works that criticize figures in their industry, it makes it so that there’s not only less of an audience seeing these critiques, but that producing these critical works is financially unsustainable. A China-developed pile-driving ship departed from a port in east China's Jiangsu Province on Sunday and is heading for Brazil, where it will take part in the building of a cross-sea bridge.

The vessel, built by China Railway Construction Bridge Engineering Bureau Group, will support the construction of the Salvador-Itaparica Bridge on Brazil's northeastern coast.

Crossing the Bay of All Saints in the state of Bahia, the bridge will have a main span of 682 meters. The project totals 46.8 kilometers, including a 12.4-kilometer cross-sea section. The main pile foundation construction area has a water depth of 64 meters and complex marine geological conditions, posing significant engineering challenges.

With an operating water depth of 70 meters, a 156-meter pile frame and a pile-lifting capacity of 700 tonnes, the ship features the world's highest pile frame, largest pile-lifting capacity and deepest operating water depth among pile-driving vessels, according to the company.

The ship combines dynamic positioning with anchor mooring to help keep it steady during construction. The system monitors wind, waves, currents and the vessel's orientation in real time and automatically adjusts thrust to stabilize the ship, according to China Railway Construction.

It will sail through the Strait of Malacca and around the Cape of Good Hope into the South Atlantic, and is expected to arrive off Brazil's northeastern coast after a voyage of about 45 days.

candidates.raw_excerpt: So far, astronomers have confirmed over 6,300 exoplanets circling a host star beyond our solar system. They range from small, rocky worlds to enormous orbs of gas like our own Jupiter or Saturn. Getting a close glimpse of these worlds remains challenging because of the unfathomable distances involved. Distinguishing the signals emanating from these exoplanets from their far brighter host stars has also been an insurmountable challenge — until now. As detailed in a yet-to-be-peer-reviewed paper , a team of astrophysicists from Harvard and the University of Oregon, Eugene, say they’ve detected radio signals directly from an exoplanet for the first time using the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa. It was first discovered in 2008 and is located 64 light-years from Earth. And no, it’s not a sign that an extraterrestrial civilization somehow living on the gas giant is trying to contact us. The team managed to isolate the signal from the exoplanet’s host star, beta Pictoris, by using the known location of quasars to determine the exact source location. Quasars are extremely magnetized and bright celestial objects at the centers of galaxies that are powered by supermassive black holes. candidates.title: SpaceX Falcon 9 launches classified mission for U.S. Space Force from West Coast
candidates.raw_excerpt: SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket soars away from Vandenberg Space Force Base on Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026, during the sunrise launch of the USSF-385 mission. Image: SpaceX A SpaceX Falcon 9 lifted off at dawn on Saturday from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California on a mission to continue deployment of a secretive U.S. military satellite constellation. Liftoff of the USSF-385 mission lifted off in dense fog at 7:00:54 a.m. PDT (10:00:54 a.m. EDT / 1400:54 UTC). The rocket took a southerly trajectory on departure from the pad at Space Launch Complex 4-East. This classified mission for the U.S. Space Force is thought to be the third in a series of flights to deploy satellites based on SpaceX’s Starshield, a version of a Starlink satellite intended for government use. SpaceX said it was not showing views of the rocket’s payload or second stage at the request of its customer. The first satellites in this particular constellation were launched from Vandenberg on USSF-366 on Aug. 15 and USSF-153 on Sept. 10. Although the Space Force revealed no details about the missions, it cataloged 23 satellites in orbit following each launch. A similar classified mission, USSF-259, headed to a different orbit on Sept. 17 and appeared to carry 17 satellites. The first stage booster, B1100, flew for a 10th time and landed on the drone ship ‘Of Course I Still Love You’, around eight and a half minutes after launch. It was the sixth and final Falcon 9 launch of the month from Vandenberg, which has become the prime site for SpaceX as it shifts its focus at Cape Canaveral to Starship operations. Just one Falcon 9 flew from the company’s East Coast launch site in September.

candidates.title: Judges Warn That AI-Generated Lawslop Is Getting So Bad It’s Threatening Courts’ Ability to Function
candidates.raw_excerpt: AI doesn’t need superintelligence to bring America’s judicial system to its knees. The proliferation of AI-generated slop paraded as legitimate legal documentation is now so bad that Florida’s second-highest appellate is sounding the alarm. In an opinion issued last week, a panel of three judges for Florida’s Fourth District Court of Appeal excoriated an attorney whose filings carried the unmistakable imprint of — in the judges’ words — “AI slop.” That assessment, first reported by Reuters , came along with a notice that the offending attorney might be referred to the Florida bar for discipline, as well as a warning that the kinds of “frivolous, scattershot arguments” generated by AI are causing serious problems for courts’ ability to process cases. “Pro se litigants and lawyers can easily abuse AI to crank out extensive and confounding documents that cause delay, annoyance, and expense to the other side,” the opinion states. “Busy courts can drown in a flood of filings that are difficult to navigate. Abusive AI filing clogs dockets and undermines the administration of justice. Courts expect more from an attorney.” As for the attorney in question, the district court found family attorney Jaclyn Soroka had filed a motion which was “legally insufficient, frivolous, and untimely.” “An AI supercomputer would struggle to find meaning in some of the prose used in this case,” the judges roared. “Counsel’s arguments need to be comprehensible to human readers — the courts, opposing counsel, and the litigants.” In an interview with Law.com , Soroka denied using any AI to produce legal documents, explaining that “in my practice of law, in all matters, I do not use artificial intelligence to generate court filings.” More on AI: OpenAI Is Now Facing Over 50 Consumer Harm and Wrongful Death Lawsuits The post Judges Warn That AI-Generated Lawslop Is Getting So Bad It’s Threatening Courts’ Ability to Function appeared first on Futurism .

candidates.title: Nvidia CEO Says AI Companies Will Be Sued to Death If Their Frontier Models Keep Doing Horrible Things

I mean, the liability’s incredible.” The solution, he says, is straightforward and motivated by existing law. “But if they believe they’re out of control, then the right answer is: don’t ship products until they’re in control,” he advised. “It is really quite that simple.” It’s a striking line from the benefactor of virtually the entire AI industry. candidates.title: What Do They Run on America's Fastest SuperComputer?
candidates.raw_excerpt: In July I paid a visit to Lawrence Livermore National Labs which hosts the fastest supercomputer in the US, a couple of months earlier it was the fastest supercomputer in the world, but Moore's law means computer supremacy is fleeting. El Capitan is an exaflop scale system, meaning is can run 10^18 calculations per second (a billion, billion), and this is measured by benchmarks that require tight cooperation between it's thousands of cores. There are datacenters with many more processors, but those may not perform at the same level because of the interconnectedness required for this kind of task. So, I wanted to look at the whole installation from bottom to top to make it clear that a supercomputer is more than having huge numbers of processors in a datacenter. candidates.title: Trump’s Stargate AI Project in Huge Trouble As $18 Billion Data Center Shrivels Toward Oblivion
candidates.raw_excerpt: Donald Trump’s $500 billion AI infrastructure project is in major trouble in New Mexico, as a pivotal data center project appears to be shriveling on the vine. Early on Thursday, the AI company Oracle sent out a notice of “force majeure” to the Blue Owl Capital, the lender backing a massive hyperscale data center critical to the president’s ambitious AI project, Bloomberg reported . Typically reserved for unexpected catastrophes like the outbreak of war, natural disaster, or massive social upheaval, Oracle invoked force majeure in order to shield itself from financial liability over the project’s failure to secure certain development permits. Zooming out, the notice is being viewed by financial commentators as an attempt by Oracle to wriggle out of responsibility for upcoming payments in the increasingly likely event that the data center isn’t finished by 2028. When — or if — the New Mexico facility goes online, the plan was for Oracle to become the primary tenant, making use of the facility’s 2.45 gigawatts of compute power for AI. A part of the $165 billion AI campus called “Project Jupiter,” the data center has run into heaps of local opposition and delays. Back in May, it was reported that Oracle had cancelled plans to erect a massive natural gas plant needed to power the facility, after developers failed to secure land use permits from both state and federal authorities. Instead, Oracle said it was pivoting to a solution using solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs), an experimental stopgap that’s never been tried at this scale. Indeed, the single largest deployment of SOFCs to-date appears to be an 80 megawatt project in South Korea — a drop in the bucket compared to the 2.45 gigawatts required if the data center is to reach its original planned potential. Oracle is the main infrastructure company behind Trump’s Stargate project, a private build-out involving OpenAI on the software side and the Japanese investment giant SoftBank on the financial management side. candidates.title: SpaceX Preparing for Most Important Launch in Company History on Monday
candidates.raw_excerpt: It feels like SpaceX’s Starship development has been in a bit of a holding pattern as of late. The company’s most recent launch in July, which was its thirteenth full-scale test in almost three and a half years, saw the spacecraft successfully deploy 20 operational satellites. But only ten out of its Super Heavy booster’s 13 Raptor engines relit during its landing, causing it to make a hard impact and explode. Now the space company is looking to finally stick the landing. This coming Monday, the company is planning to launch its fourteenth test flight, “ pending regulatory approval .” The plan is to have Starship circle the Earth a full six times over ten hours at an altitude of 171 miles before lightly touching down. It’s almost certainly the biggest test of the launch platform yet, and arguably the most important launch in the company’s history. Proving its orbital flight capabilities is mission critical if SpaceX ever wants Starship to deliver satellites at a regular cadence. It’s also a key aspect of NASA’s planned Artemis 3 mission, which is currently slated for 2027 , a key stepping stone in the space agency’s ambitions to return astronauts to the lunar surface. But give the sheer number of challenges SpaceX still has to overcome, from reliably entering orbit to sticking the landing of both its spacecraft and its booster, SpaceX may need to buy itself some more time before it can get NASA astronauts aboard its spacecraft in the Earth’s orbit next year. SpaceX successfully conducted a full wet dress rehearsal earlier this week ahead of its Monday launch attempt. Without igniting any engines, the company’s team ran through the countdown procedures to ensure everything’s ready. candidates.title: With PRIMA, NASA will try to build a billion-dollar space telescope in record time
candidates.raw_excerpt: The first in a new class of space telescopes is on track to reach the launch pad in the early 2030s, NASA announced this week. The PRIMA mission will be the first of NASA's Probe Explorers, a new line of observatories intended to do more science for less money. The agency's space telescopes typically fall into lower-cost "Explorer-class" missions, with cost caps in the range of a few hundred million dollars, or flagship observatories like the recently launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, which came with a price tag of some $4.3 billion. With the Probe Explorers, NASA officials seek to find a better balance between the smaller Explorer missions and multibillion-dollar flagships. NASA has studied potential Probe Explorer mission concepts for several years after an independent panel of scientists recommended the new mission category. But it wasn't clear until recently whether NASA's science budget, which is under pressure from the Trump administration , would be sufficient to actually start developing one. candidates.title: Starfish Space’s Debut Otter Vehicle Hitches a Ride on SpaceX’s Transporter-18 Launch
candidates.raw_excerpt: Starfish Space will launch its first Otter satellite servicing vehicle next month aboard SpaceX’s Transporter-18 rideshare mission, the company announced Thursday. Starfish Space designed Otter vehicles with a flexible architecture for life extension and end-of-life disposal missions. The company said they can operate within multiple orbital regimes and support spacecraft not originally designed to be serviced. The first Otter scheduled for launch in October will conduct Starfish’s Small Spacecraft Propulsion and Inspection Capability (SSPICY) mission for NASA. Following launch, Starfish will commission the spacecraft and prepare to provide commercial services in low Earth orbit. “This is the moment Otter becomes real. It’s no longer something we’re designing for the future. The first Otter is built, it has a customer and a mission, and it’s going to space. That’s a huge moment for Starfish and for everyone who has worked to get us here,” said Austin Link, co-founder of Starfish. By building upon the technologies, systems, and operational experience developed through the Haven‑1 program, Vast aims to develop a scalable path toward lunar infrastructure, scientific discovery, and long‑term human exploration. candidates.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Says That Sacrificing Our Children’s Minds to AI Is a Price He’s Willing to Pay
candidates.raw_excerpt: With so much hype about the future of AI safety, it can be easy to overlook the harms AI is causing in the here and now. On the consumer side, the impact generative AI has on the developing mind is becoming increasingly clear: students are losing critical thinking skills as chatbots become cognitive crutches , spurning human friends in favor of AI companions , and even turning to self-harm when their AI-relationships go awry. Few tech executives have acknowledged these urgent harms. Instead they’re choosing to push a narrative around the hypothetical threat of a runaway “superintelligence” which humans can no longer control. That’s why it’s notable that Jensen Huang, CEO of the AI chipmaking titan Nvidia, was recently grilled on the cognitive harm AI is inflicting on students. Unfortunately, his response was far from reassuring, providing further proof of the AI industry’s blatant disregard for the wellbeing of ordinary people. Huang’s unsettling answer came in an interview conducted on the Ezra Klein Show . Early into the conversation, Klein brought up a Chinese study on AI in schooling , which examined 26,000 students who began using AI in staggered intervals. Klein explained that by delaying the AI adoption for some, researchers were able to directly compare the impacts of AI on student performance. Though students were able to complete work faster with AI, the study found compelling evidence that the cognitive skills needed to complete school work melted away, resulting in lower exam scores in the long-term. In response, Huang agreed that student cognition is getting much worse. “Try to get a kid to do long division right now. The multiplication table is starting to be forgotten. candidates.raw_excerpt: HOUSTON, TX — Iridium ($IRDM) shareholders voted overwhelmingly yesterday to approve the company’s proposed acquisition by Rocket Lab ($RKLB). According to Rocket Lab CFO Adam Spice, there’s more M&A on the horizon.  In the shareholders meeting, 99.6% of votes were cast in favor of the buyout, putting Rocket Lab one step closer to owning the satcom giant. The deal is expected to close in mid-2027 for ~$54 per Iridium share—in a mix of cash and RKLB stock.  Gotta have it: The Iridium purchase is the latest in a string of increasingly large buyouts that started before the company went public via SPAC in 2021. The acquisitions have given Rocket Lab a breadth of new capabilities, including flight software, satellite separation systems, space solar power products, electro-optical and infrared sensors, laser communications terminals, and in-space robotics systems. And the company isn’t done buying just yet.  Speaking virtually at Payload’s Off World event in Houston yesterday, Rocket Lab CFO Adam Spice confirmed that the company is considering more M&A opportunities to continue expanding its capabilities, and win larger, more impactful contracts.  “Going forward, when you look at our government customers, they’re looking for more than just one thing,” Spice said. “Whether that’s Earth observation capabilities, whether it’s different kinds of sensors for scientific or national security purposes. We’re going to be going out continuing to pick those capabilities up…We’re not stopping at L-band communications with Iridium. We’re rather building on that to be able to offer more and more to the market.” The decision to build or buy, however, will be met on a case-by-case basis, according to Spice, who added that the company’s tech is a healthy mix between the two. Wales said this investment was led by his fellow cofounder Cameron Borumand—a far cry from the company’s first space investment in 2024. In January 2024, FUSE dipped its toe into the space industry for the first time, leading the $6M seed round for Quindar . The company—which develops mission management software for spacecraft—allowed investors to fall back on their software background while exploring space.  “We had a massive argument in the partner meeting about, should we even be doing Quindar,” Wales said. “Sure enough, it ended up opening into a much bigger market.” FUSE later joined the seed round for Starcloud, making its second space investment.  And—while FUSE’s space investments now stretch beyond Seattle—the firm is still working to grow the space ecosystem around its home base. candidates.title: Callisto Reusable Rocket Demonstrator Takes Shape Ahead of 2027 Hop Test
candidates.raw_excerpt: Credit: DLR The German Aerospace Center (DLR) has completed final testing of the nose cone for the Callisto reusable rocket demonstrator, with the hardware now set to be transferred to France for final integration. DLR has also confirmed that the demonstrator’s initial hop test has slipped to 2027, a delay first hinted at in a French space agency (CNES) procurement notice published in September 2025. DLR announced on 11 September that the nose cone had successfully completed acceptance testing. The carbon-fibre structure will be delivered to the French space agency CNES and APCO Technologies for integration into Callisto’s top block before it is shipped to the Guiana Space Centre. A “super El Niño,” a heightened version of a recurring natural climate pattern that triggers unusually hot temperatures , has resulted in the perfect storm, endangering a staggering number of lives with extreme weather. The prognosis is grim, if not catastrophic. According to the latest report by scientists at the research organization Climate Impact Lab, some 451,000 lives “will be lost due to heat in the first half of this El Niño, compared to a normal year.” “The estimate of 451,000 people is such a large number that it can be numbing, but it is made up of parents and children, grandparents and neighbors, people going to work, caring for families, and living their lives,” said cofounder and University of Chicago professor Michael Greenstone in an accompanying statement . It doesn’t bode well, considering the current weather pattern will stick around until at least spring 2027, meaning that the death toll could “grow even higher, particularly as impacts such as higher-than-average temperatures and heat-related deaths will linger into June and July” next year. Areas of the globe hit particularly hard are largely found in the southern hemisphere. Regions across northern Africa, South East Asia, and Latin America are expected to see the “largest increase in heat-related deaths over the next six months.” The most impacted countries, as identified by Climate Impact Lab, are Nigeria, Indonesia, Sudan, India, and Brazil. However, we’re not entirely helpless. With the help of humanitarian organizations, governments can send out heat warnings, reach out to vulnerable populations, provide cooling centers and hydration stations, and expand health system capacity as needed. “This report allows decision makers to see exactly where emergency actions can be taken now to save tens of thousands of lives in the coming months,” Greenstone explained in the statement. candidates.raw_excerpt: Earlier this month, OpenAI announced that it had found a solution for one of the biggest unsolved problems in math, the Navier-Stokes equations, by directing 10,000 of its powerful AI agents to work on the enigma for 88 hours straight. It was an occasion fraught with controversy , however, as mathematicians accused the company of essentially stealing their work. That controversy is still rippling through the math world. But what has the AI’s solution taught us? Not a lot, as it turns out, because the proof it wrote, while technically correct, is borderline incomprehensible. “So far it’s been very difficult to really extract any human understanding from this new AI proof,” James Maynard, an Oxford mathematician, told NPR . “The paper is not written for humans,” echoed Javier Gómez-Serrano, a mathematician at Brown University who uses AI in his own research. The AI’s proof could help the field after “some serious re-writing,” he added, but “as of today, the paper doesn’t teach us much.” The Navier-Stokes equations mathematically describe how fluids, ranging from a rush of wind to the churn of ocean currents, move and behave. They’ve been used for nearly two centuries with reliable results, but why they work remains something of a mystery. Scientists have been eager to push the equations to their limits and see if their predictions could reach a breaking point where they describe a scenario that makes no sense in the real world. Reifying the equation’s importance, the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000 listed the Navier-Stokes as one of its six Millennium Problems, with the prize for solving it at $1 million. OpenAI claimed that its swarm of AI agents identified a scenario in which the fluids accelerate to an infinite velocity, creating a “blow up” or singularity — something, of course, that’s impossible in the physical universe. candidates.title: Microsoft Patents Technique for Inserting Ads Into Videogames While You’re Playing Them
candidates.raw_excerpt: Trying to escape the increasingly dystopian real world with a jaunt into the virtual one? A new system patented by Microsoft might make that easier said than done. Recently, Microsoft published a brand-new patent application for an “ad credit” system meant to seamlessly pump paid promotional material into video games. That’s according to Respawn First , which noted that the system would rely on signals relayed by the game engine to choose opportune times to serve gamers in-game commercials. These would vary from game-to-game, but generally encompass pre-existing events like boss fights, loading screens, and transitions out of cutscenes. When the system receives a positive signal, it stops the game in its tracks to serve either a video ad or static image, which also resets a timer counting down until the system goes back on the hunt for another in-game signal. “In non-interactive audiovisual content such periodic breaks can be placed at a variety of predictable times in the content without adversely affecting the user experience,” the Microsoft patent declares. “However, interactive software applications which stream interactive audiovisual content can provide a more varied user experience and predicting when to suspend interaction and present promoted audiovisual content can be challenging.” Called “Contextually Aware Management of Interactive Software Application Access,” it isn’t known if Microsoft has begun rolling it out to games, or if it even plans to. Overall, it appears geared toward free-to-play games on the Xbox and PC, Respawn notes — though given the slow creep of publisher-driven mechanisms like microtransactions , it may be just a matter of time before the context-aware ad system makes its way to paid titles as well.
